name: FOCACCIA RED HANDED BURGER (on focaccia with beets)

recipe.history:
Focaccia is one of the oldest breads in the Western culinary tradition, predating the rise of modern leavened bread by centuries. The Romans made a flat, oil-enriched bread called panis focacius — panis meaning bread, focacius derived from focus, meaning hearth — baked directly on the coals or in the ashes of a fire. It was the bread of soldiers and travelers, practical and sustaining. In the Liguria region of northwestern Italy, focaccia became an art form: the Genoese focaccia — thick, pillowy, dimpled with fingertips, drenched in excellent olive oil, and sprinkled with flaky sea salt — is one of the great breads of the world. Bakeries in Genoa open before dawn and sell focaccia warm from the oven, and locals eat it for breakfast dipped in cappuccino, which sounds improbable until you try it. The bread's open, spongy crumb absorbs olive oil with almost greedy enthusiasm, and its thick crust provides the structural integrity to serve as a burger bun without collapsing under the weight of toppings.

Beets are an ancient root vegetable consumed since at least the time of ancient Babylon, cultivated widely across the Mediterranean and eventually spreading throughout Europe, where they developed into both table beets (red and golden) and sugar beets. They arrived in America with European settlers and became deeply embedded in Eastern European immigrant cuisine — borscht, pickled beets, and beet salads were transported to the new world by communities from Poland, Russia, Ukraine, and Scandinavia. In contemporary American cooking, roasted beets had a dramatic resurgence in the farm-to-table era of the 2000s, appearing on restaurant menus alongside goat cheese and walnuts in a combination that became something of a cliché, but a delicious one. On a burger, roasted beets provide earthiness, sweetness, moisture, and their indelible crimson color — the 'red handed' of this recipe's name.

The first time I served this burger to friends, one of them looked at her hands after assembly and found them stained deep magenta from the beets. She held them up and said, completely straight-faced, 'I've been red handed.' I laughed so hard I nearly dropped the burger. Beet juice is extraordinarily persistent on skin and on cutting boards — I learned to use a dedicated plastic cutting board for beets after permanently staining my wooden one a color that might generously be described as 'unsettling.' The trick with roasted beets is patience: they need at least an hour in a hot oven, individually wrapped in foil with olive oil, before their skins slip off easily and their interior becomes tender and sweet. There are no shortcuts that produce the same result.

Focaccia is a bold, oily, assertive bread — it makes demands on everything between its halves. Only a medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit has the presence and juiciness to meet focaccia on equal terms. The bread's spongy crumb will absorb the patty's rendered fat eagerly, creating a kind of communion between bread and beef that only works when the beef has fat to offer. An overcooked, dry patty disappears inside focaccia — it becomes filler. A medium-rare patty is a partner. Use a thermometer, cook to 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, rest for three minutes, and the focaccia will reward you for your respect.
ingredients: 80ml extra-virgin olive oil (divided: 40ml for dough, 40ml for pan and topping)
225g fresh goat cheese, at room temperature
instructions: 1. Roast the beets: Preheat oven to 400°F (200°C). Individually wrap each beet in foil with a drizzle of olive oil and a pinch of salt. Roast 60 to 75 minutes until a skewer slides in with no resistance. Unwrap, cool 15 minutes, then rub skins off with paper towels. Slice into rounds 1/4 inch thick. Toss with balsamic vinegar, remaining olive oil, and thyme. Set aside.

2. Make the focaccia: Combine warm water, yeast, and sugar in a large bowl. Let sit 5 minutes. Add flour, salt, and 40ml olive oil. Mix until a sticky dough forms. Knead in the bowl by repeatedly stretching and folding for 5 minutes. Cover and rest 1 hour at room temperature. Oil a 9x13-inch baking pan generously with remaining olive oil. Transfer dough to the pan and stretch it to fill the pan as best you can. Cover and rest 45 minutes until puffed. Dimple the surface aggressively with your fingertips. Drizzle with the remaining olive oil from the recipe. Scatter rosemary leaves and flaky sea salt over the surface. Bake at 425°F (220°C) 20 to 25 minutes until deeply golden. Cool completely before cutting into 4 square burger-sized portions, then halve each portion horizontally.

3. Make the whipped goat cheese: Beat goat cheese with an electric mixer or in a food processor until smooth and fluffy, about 2 minutes. Add heavy cream and beat until light. Fold in lemon juice, chives, salt, and pepper. Refrigerate.

4. Prepare the patties: Combine ground beef with thyme, salt, and pepper. Mix gently. Divide into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Shape into square patties slightly larger than the focaccia portions, 3/4 inch thick. Make a thumb dimple in the center. Refrigerate 15 minutes before cooking.

5. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties 3 minutes undisturbed. Flip and lay a slice of fontina on each. Cook 2 to 2.5 minutes more until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). Remove and rest 3 minutes.
6. While patties rest, warm the beet slices briefly in the same skillet over medium heat, about 2 minutes.
7. Toast focaccia cut sides in the skillet fat over medium heat until golden and crisp, about 2 minutes.

8. Assemble: Spread whipped goat cheese generously on both focaccia halves. Place a small nest of arugula on the bottom half. Set the rested patty with melted fontina on the arugula. Layer 3 or 4 roasted beet rounds on top. Drizzle balsamic glaze lightly over the beets. Finish with flaky sea salt. Cap with the top focaccia half and serve immediately.
